summary: Defines instance digests for HTTP, letting a message carry a checksum of the whole resource rather than just the body piece sent, and allowing more than one digest algorithm. It extends the idea of Content-MD5. It was replaced by RFC 9530.

eli5.summary: A checksum is a fingerprint for a file. This lets a web server send a fingerprint of the whole file even if you only got a part of it. It has been replaced by RFC 9530.

questions: how to verify partial file integrity
subtitle: Standard checksums for the whole web file, not just the piece you received

tldr.problem: HTTP's Content-MD5 header covers only the body sent in a single response, not the complete file. When a client reconstructs a file from range requests (partial downloads) or delta encodings (compressed updates), Content-MD5 cannot verify the integrity of the reassembled whole.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds two new HTTP headers: Want-Digest (to request checksums) and Digest (to send them). It also supports multiple digest algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, etc.) instead of just MD5, and includes a negotiation mechanism so clients can ask servers which algorithms they prefer.
tldr.outcome: Web clients can now verify complete file integrity across partial transfers and delta updates. The RFC was later replaced by RFC 9530, which updates the security guarantees and adds additional digest algorithms.

facts.label: Digest algorithms supported
facts.value: MD5, SHA, UNIXsum, UNIXcksum (extensible via IANA)

today: RFC 3230 is an Internet Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 9530, which strengthens security recommendations, adds SHA-256 and other modern algorithms, and clarifies the digest mechanism's limitations. Modern HTTP clients and servers should use RFC 9530 for integrity checking in partial transfers and delta-encoded responses.

sections.title: The Problem with Content-MD5
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 includes a Content-MD5 header that allows servers to send an MD5 checksum of the response body. However, this header covers only the entity in that single message, not the entire resource or instance.

Two common scenarios expose this weakness. First, when a server sends a 206 (Partial Content) response to a range request, the client may combine the cached earlier part with the new partial content to form the complete file. If either the cache or the new part was corrupted, Content-MD5 (computed only on the partial content) would not detect it. Second, when delta encoding is used (where the server sends only the differences between a new file version and an old one), the client must apply the delta to reconstruct the full file. Again, Content-MD5 covers only the delta, not the reconstructed result.
sections.eli5: Imagine downloading a big file in two pieces. The first piece has a fingerprint, the second piece has a fingerprint, but there's no way to check if when you glue them together you get the right complete file.

sections.title: Goals and Design
sections.content:
This RFC addresses three goals: digests that cover the entire instance (not just a message part), support for multiple digest algorithms beyond MD5 (such as SHA-1), and a negotiation mechanism so clients can request digests rather than servers deciding unilaterally whether to compute them.

The solution does not attempt to protect HTTP headers themselves, authenticate the message source, provide privacy, or enforce access controls. Those are separate concerns better handled by other mechanisms like HTTPS or digest authentication. Instance digests focus solely on data integrity for the message body.
sections.eli5: The goal is simple: let the client ask for a fingerprint using a method they understand, and have the server send a checksum of the whole thing, not just what's in this one message.

sections.title: What is an Instance?
sections.content:
The RFC defines a key term, instance: the entity that would be returned in a status-200 response to a GET request at the current time for the selected variant of a resource, after applying content codings but before applying instance manipulations (like range requests) or transfer codings.

An instance is distinct from the entity in a single HTTP message. For example, if a resource is 10 MB and a client requests bytes 1000-2000, the entity is 1000 bytes (the range), but the instance is the full 10 MB. Similarly, if delta encoding compresses the differences, the entity is the delta, but the instance is the complete reconstructed file.

Entity tags in HTTP are associated with instances: the same strong entity tag should never be assigned to two different instances of a resource.
sections.eli5: An 'instance' is the true complete file on the server. An 'entity' is just the piece you're getting right now. The digest should be for the whole file, not just the piece.

sections.title: The Digest and Want-Digest Headers
sections.content:
The Want-Digest header allows a client to request that a server include instance digests in its response. The header lists one or more digest algorithms and quality values (qvalues) indicating preference:

Want-Digest: md5;q=0.3, sha;q=1

This example says the client prefers SHA but will accept MD5 with lower preference. Servers SHOULD choose the algorithm with the highest qvalue when sending the Digest header in response.

The Digest header carries the actual digest(s). It may contain multiple instance-digest values, each in the form algorithm=encoded-value:

Digest: SHA=thvDyvhfIqlvFe+A9MYgxAfm1q5=

Digest values are encoded according to the algorithm: MD5 and SHA use base64, while UNIX checksums use ASCII decimal strings. A server can send multiple digests (e.g., both MD5 and SHA) in a single response.
sections.eli5: You send a message saying 'I can check fingerprints using these methods.' The server picks one and sends back the fingerprint in that format.

sections.title: Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC initially defines four digest algorithm values, all case-insensitive:

  • MD5: The MD5 algorithm, output base64-encoded.
  • SHA: The SHA-1 algorithm, output base64-encoded. SHA-1 produces a stronger digest than MD5 (160 bits vs 128 bits) and is more resistant to collision attacks.
  • UNIXsum: The output of the UNIX sum command, a 16-bit checksum, output as an ASCII decimal string.
  • UNIXcksum: The output of the UNIX cksum command, a 32-bit CRC, output as an ASCII decimal string.

The IANA registry allows additional algorithms to be registered if documented in an RFC or other permanent reference. New algorithms must encode their output as a quoted string or avoid semicolons and commas in the encoding.
sections.eli5: Different fingerprinting methods have different trade-offs: MD5 is fast but old, SHA is stronger, and UNIX commands are simple but weak.

sections.title: Negotiating Content-MD5
sections.content:
The RFC includes a backward-compatibility mechanism for HTTP/1.1's Content-MD5 header. A new pseudo-algorithm called contentMD5 can appear in Want-Digest with a qvalue. A non-zero qvalue indicates the client wishes to receive Content-MD5 headers; a zero qvalue (e.g., contentMD5;q=0) indicates the client will ignore them.

This allows clients to control whether servers waste resources computing MD5 digests, especially important since computing digests has CPU costs and transmitting them uses bandwidth.
sections.eli5: If the server supports the old Content-MD5 header, you can use Want-Digest to tell it whether you want it or not.
